hits.body: A later business request returning HTTP 200 demonstrates recovery for that request at that time. It does not prove service health during an earlier incident or reveal why the earlier request failed. Avoid extending one observation into a continuous availability claim.

hits.title: Cart validation and HTTP client errors
hits.heading: Invalid carts
hits.body: The checkout schema accepts the book item and quantities from one through ten. A missing or invalid field, zero quantity, or quantity eleven is rejected with HTTP 422 before business processing. Extra fields are forbidden. Invalid input is not evidence of a failing dependency.

hits.title: Cart validation and HTTP client errors
hits.heading: Client errors versus dependency failures
hits.body: HTTP 422 describes invalid cart input. HTTP 502 describes checkout failing to complete a downstream call. Compare the response, dependency field, and correlated logs. Do not attribute a rejected cart to payment or inventory without observations of those services.

hits.title: Missing logs and insufficient evidence
hits.heading: Empty results versus unavailable sources
hits.body: A successful query with zero matching records differs from a timeout, unreadable log file, or unavailable service telemetry. Empty results cover only the requested service, time window, and retained data. An unavailable source provides no evidence that requests were healthy.

hits.title: Missing logs and insufficient evidence
hits.heading: Retention and truncated evidence
hits.body: Local logs rotate and queries return a bounded number of records. Truncated responses may omit relevant errors; older coverage after rotation cannot be guaranteed. Preserve truncation and the query window. Do not describe retained records as a complete incident history.

hits.title: Missing logs and insufficient evidence
hits.heading: Abstain when support is missing
hits.body: Separate observed facts from possible explanations. A runbook provides general guidance, not a current incident observation. If no available observation distinguishes competing causes, mark the cause inconclusive and suggest permitted read-only checks. A retrieval score is not a calibrated probability.

hits.title: Dependency timeouts and network reachability
hits.heading: Response failure versus transport failure
hits.body: A downstream request failed record with an HTTP status means an error response was received. A downstream request unavailable record without a status indicates a transport problem such as timeout, name resolution failure, or refused connection. This generic message does not distinguish those causes. Do not claim an unmeasured timeout duration.

hits.title: Dependency timeouts and network reachability
hits.heading: Bounded requests
hits.body: Checkout configures a one-second HTTP client timeout for dependency calls and does not retry transactions automatically. Compare recorded duration, neighboring requests, and downstream logs. The configured timeout does not prove that every unavailable response was a timeout. Timeout categories apply to phases of the HTTP operation rather than guaranteeing a one-second total duration.

hits.title: Dependency timeouts and network reachability
hits.heading: Read-only follow-up
hits.body: Compare dependency health, request errors, and available configuration evidence. A later successful response does not prove connectivity during the incident. Missing network observations should be listed as missing evidence rather than converted into a specific transport diagnosis.

hits.title: Deployment timing and causal investigation
hits.heading: Timing is not causation
hits.body: An error beginning near a deployment is a useful lead, not proof of a regression. Compare affected and unaffected services, request IDs, signatures, and observations before and after the change. Determine whether the deployed component is on the failing dependency path.

hits.title: Deployment timing and causal investigation
hits.heading: Missing deployment history
hits.body: This release has no deployment-history tool. If deployment events cannot be observed, state that limitation instead of inventing a timeline. A user's description of a change should be distinguished from independently collected deployment evidence.

hits.title: Deployment timing and causal investigation
hits.heading: Applicability of guidance
hits.body: Use guidance for the correct environment and release. Older architecture may describe dependencies that no longer exist. Cite the document revision and preserve the observation window. Relevant documentation suggests checks but cannot establish that a particular change caused this incident.

hits.title: Request ID correlation across HTTP services
hits.heading: Joining observations
hits.body: Use request_id to join checkout, inventory, and payment logs in the same observation window. Accepted IDs contain exactly 32 lowercase hexadecimal characters. Invalid supplied IDs are replaced at ingress. Timestamp proximity alone does not establish that two errors belong to the same request.

hits.title: Request ID correlation across HTTP services
hits.heading: Partial correlation
hits.body: A matching request ID supports following a dependency boundary. A missing match can arise from log retention, an incorrect time window, a transport failure, or a request that never reached the downstream service. Preserve missing evidence; do not invent a trace or assume downstream success.

hits.title: Read-only investigation and transaction retry safety
hits.heading: No automatic transaction retries
hits.body: Checkout does not automatically retry inventory or payment transactions. The investigator's tools only read observations and reviewed guidance. Suggested verification steps must not become automatic restarts, configuration changes, repeated charges, or shell execution.

hits.title: Read-only investigation and transaction retry safety
hits.heading: Guidance is not evidence
hits.body: A procedure describes what an operator might verify. It does not establish that its described failure is happening now. Link current observations to each hypothesis, acknowledge contradictory evidence, and leave the underlying cause inconclusive when available signals cannot distinguish alternatives.

hits.title: Shopping service dependencies and boundaries
hits.heading: Request flow
hits.body: Checkout calls inventory availability first, then payment processing. Inventory success does not establish payment success. If inventory fails, checkout stops without calling payment. Use the dependency name as well as the response status to localize the failing boundary.

hits.title: Shopping service dependencies and boundaries
hits.heading: Request correlation
hits.body: Checkout propagates a valid request ID to inventory and payment. Compare records from the same request and incident window. A shared ID links observations but does not identify the underlying cause. Match service, timestamp, dependency, and status before correlating unrelated errors.

hits.title: Shopping service dependencies and boundaries
hits.heading: Supported architecture
hits.body: This release is an HTTP shopping simulation. It has no real payment gateway, order database, customer accounts, or stock reservation. Do not infer database connection exhaustion or external financial failures without an applicable architecture revision and actual observations. Process health is separate from successful business requests.

hits.title: Operational log adapter availability
hits.heading: Adapter failure outcomes
hits.body: source_timeout, source_unreachable, source_http_error, and invalid_source_response mean logs are unavailable. These adapter errors do not prove target application failure or target health. A successful empty query is a different outcome. Preserve the source error, query scope, and truncation status.

hits.title: Operational log adapter availability
hits.heading: Bounded evidence reads
hits.body: The adapter permits a fixed configured source URL, a service allowlist, ordered incident windows no longer than an hour, at most 100 returned records, and a response-size cap. It does not accept arbitrary SQL, shell commands, or user-selected destinations.
